# Teacher checkpoints — separate,notaccess-protected
Traffic outcomes, in order: allow R1, deny R4, allow R2, allow R3, deny by default, deny by default. An early broad Visitor allow incorrectly permits internal TCP port 443 traffic, demonstrating first-match shadowing. UDP port 443 is deliberately outside the model; HTTP/3 may need an explicit policy. DNS, DHCP, connection state and IPv6 are also outside this model.

Role outcomes, in order: True, True, False, True, False, True. The model predicts only the supplied tuples; it does not authenticate users or verify actual record scope. Network reachability does not grant export rights. A source IP address does not establish a person's identity.

Controls: logs support evidence but do not prevent events by themselves. Anti-malware is limited by visibility and detection. Firewalls and ACLs depend on traffic path and rule order. An IPS blocks traffic, but false positives can harm availability. A VPN protects its tunnel, not a compromised endpoint. Training and codes of conduct need technical and process support. Physical controls reduce physical exposure. MFA does not repair excessive permissions; a backup does not reverse disclosure. Accept justified combinations of controls.

Response cards: for credential/export concerns, verify role, session and activity; use authorised session/access containment, repair permissions and retest permitted and prohibited actions. For ransomware, preserve evidence and isolate under an authorised plan; investigate cause and scope, verify a trusted restore and retain uncertainty about disclosure. For an IPS false positive, corroborate the legitimate workflow and review or tune narrowly rather than allowing all traffic. For a stolen laptop, verify encryption, session and device state and use an authorised device/account response; do not assume that a password alone protects data.

These are practice checkpoints. A passing model is not proof of production enforcement. Independent review and actual learner explanations remain necessary.
